title: Build a Chat App
summary: Design Parley's messaging interview style: WebSocket gateways, ordered storage per conversation, at-least-once delivery with dedupe, offline push, receipts, presence and groups.

goals.text: Size connections, message rate and storage
Keep one order per conversation with sequence numbers
Deliver at least once, then dedupe
Handle offline users, receipts, presence and groups

steps.title: What a chat app must guarantee
body: The prompt: “Design a chat app.” Parley needs 1:1 and group chats, messages that arrive in real time when you're online and wait for you when you're not, and one agreed order in every conversation.
Two guarantees carry most of the design: a message is never lost, and it's never shown twice. Ticks and presence are nice-to-haves, but they shape the protocol, so note them now.

card.title: Requirements
lines: **must**: 1:1 and group chats (≤ 500)
**must**: delivered in real time when online
**must**: stored; delivered later when offline
**must**: same order for everyone in a chat
**nice**: sent / delivered / read ticks
**nice**: online & last-seen presence
# never lose a message; never show one twice

steps.title: Sockets, not requests
body: With 50 million daily users sending 40 messages each, that's about 23,000 messages a second, peaking near 70,000. Each message is about 200 bytes, so roughly 150 TB a year of history.
The unusual number is connections: 20 million phones online at once, each holding a socket open. At ~50,000 sockets per server that's ~400 gateway machines, before we've processed a single message.

card.title: Back of the envelope
lines: 50 M daily users · **20 M online** at peak
40 messages/user/day → 2 B/day
1 open socket per online device → 20 M sockets
~50k sockets per gateway → **~400 gateways**

steps.title: A small protocol over WebSockets
body: Polling every few seconds would waste battery and still feel slow. Instead, each device opens one WebSocket and keeps it open; the server can push to it any time.
The client tags each message with its own client_msg_id. The server replies with an ack carrying the message's seq. A plain REST call fetches everything after a given seq for catching up.

card.title: The protocol
lines: → send { conv_id, client_msg_id, body }
← ack { client_msg_id, seq }
← msg { conv_id, seq, sender, body }
→ receipt { conv_id, seq, delivered | read }
GET /v1/conversations/{id}/messages?after_seq=
# frames over one long-lived socket; REST to catch up

steps.title: Gateways and a registry
body: Gateways only hold sockets: thousands of mostly idle connections each. Behind them, a stateless Chat service does the work: store the message, then deliver it.

But Ines is on gateway 1 and Tomás on gateway 2. To deliver, the Chat service asks a session registry (a Redis map of user → gateway, written when a device connects) and forwards the frame to gateway 2, which pushes it down Tomás's socket.
changes: + Chat service, session registry, message store

steps.title: Deep dive: one order per chat
body: Ines sends “Running late” then “Start without me”. Ordering by timestamp fails: two servers' clocks can disagree by milliseconds, so the messages may swap. In a group, two members can send at the same instant.

Instead, all writes for one conversation go to one Chat service owner (by hash of conv_id), which assigns the next sequence number. Messages are stored partitioned by conversation and sorted by seq, so history is one fast range read.

callout.text: You only need order within a conversation. A global order across all chats would be expensive and nobody would notice it.

changes: + Panel: messages table keyed by (conv_id, seq)

card.title: Messages table
lines: partition key: **conv_id**
sort key: **seq** ↑ · sender, client_msg_id, body
seq: per-chat counter, assigned on write
= every member sees the same order
# not timestamps: device and server clocks drift
# read: WHERE conv_id = ? AND seq > last_seen

steps.title: The ack that never arrived
body: Ines's train enters a tunnel. Her message reaches the server and is stored, but the ack is lost on the way back. From her phone's point of view, the message may not have arrived.
If the app gives up, a message might be lost. If it simply sends again, Tomás sees “On my way” twice. Networks can't tell you which of the two happened.

steps.title: At least once, then dedupe
body: The phone keeps unsent messages in a local outbox and retries until it gets an ack: at-least-once delivery. The server stores the message before acking, so an ack always means “safe”.

Duplicates are removed by idempotency: the Chat service remembers each client_msg_id per conversation. A retry of a known id gets the original seq back instead of a new row. Clients dedupe incoming frames by seq too.

callout.text: Exactly-once delivery over a network isn't possible; exactly-once effect is: at-least-once + dedupe.

changes: ~ Store keeps one row per message

steps.title: When Tomás is offline
body: Tomás's phone is in his pocket with the app closed. The registry has no session for him, so the Chat service hands the message to a Push service, which notifies the phone through Apple's or Google's push network.
The message is already safe in the store. When Tomás opens the app, it reconnects and asks for everything after the last seq it saw, then switches to live frames. The push only carries a preview.

card.title: Back online: sync
lines: Tomás opens the app → socket to any gateway
GET …/messages?after_seq=41
= gets 42–57 in order, then live frames
# the push holds a preview only
# the message store is the source of truth

steps.title: Ticks and presence
body: Receipts reuse the same pipeline as messages. One tick: the server acked (stored). Two ticks: Tomás's device acked the frame. Read: his app reports the highest seq on screen, and one number covers every earlier message.

Presence is a key in the registry that each heartbeat renews, expiring after 30 seconds of silence. Telling every contact about every change would dwarf the message traffic, so it's only sent to people who have that chat open.
changes: ~ Delivery round trip returns as a receipt

card.title: Receipts & presence
lines: ✓ sent: stored, seq assigned (the ack)
✓✓ delivered: Tomás's device acked the frame
read: app reports last_read_seq
= receipts are tiny messages on the same path
presence: heartbeat every 20 s, key TTL 30 s
# push presence only to chats on screen

steps.title: Groups, and where it bends
body: Ines posts in a 300-member group. The message is stored once; the Chat service looks up all members in one batched registry call, then sends one batch per gateway, not 300 separate frames. Offline members get a push.

Then stress-test: very large channels should let members pull instead; a gateway crash means 50,000 phones reconnect at once, so clients back off with random jitter; one very busy chat becomes a hot partition.
changes: ~ Chat service fans out per gateway

card.title: Where it bends
lines: ! groups: store once, send 1 batch per gateway
! 100k-member channels: members pull instead
! gateway dies → 50k reconnect: jittered backoff
! one very busy chat → one hot partition
! presence storms → only for contacts on screen

steps.title: Parley, end to end
body:
• Gateways hold sockets; a registry maps users to gateways.
  • Per-conversation seq gives one order; store by (conv_id, seq).
  • Store, then ack; clients retry from an outbox; dedupe by client_msg_id.
  • Offline: push a preview, sync from the last seq on reconnect.
  • Receipts are tiny messages; presence is a heartbeat with a TTL.
  • Groups: write once, fan out per gateway; big channels pull.
